description: We’re four third-year students at Forward College studying data science, business analytics, and business management. We're studying in Lisbon, Paris, and Berlin, where we’re spending our final year and taking part in the regional NASA Space Apps Challenge. We share a curiosity about what patterns in data can tell us about the world and how those insights can inform real decisions.
summary:
D² Detective (Data Detectives) is a gamified data visualization that employs eight NASA Earth-observation variables, spanning twenty years (2005-2024), to engage data- and science-curious members of the public in evidence-based environmental reasoning.
Participants assume the role of “data detectives” and are tasked with selecting one of six regions in which to plant a single Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris). To reach a decision, they explore each region interactively, judge which variables are relevant to tree growth, and examine temporal trends and summary statistics.
The project aims to show how environmental variables interact with one another and jointly influence a tangible ecological outcome. By linking abstract datasets to a concrete decision, D² Detective offers an accessible entry point to data literacy and Earth-system science. The approach is also extensible to broader applications, including climate change impacts, deforestation, and vegetation restoration.
details:
D Squared Detectives

Figure 1: Screenshot of landing page in website.

What it does and how it works

D² Detective: The Scots Pine Case is a browser game that teaches people to read Earth-observation data like a detective. The player meets a Scots pine, one of Europe’s most widespread trees, and has to decide where to plant a single seed. The choices are six very different regions: Brandenburg/Berlin, the Scottish Highlands, Finnish Lapland, the Valais Alps, Central Spain, and the Kazakh steppe. As seen below in Figure 2.

Figure 2: Screenshot of the confidential mission briefing and the Scots pine specimen card in website.

Each region has an evidence board built from 20 years (2005–2024) of real NASA data:

  • Seven climate variables from GLDAS, accessed through NASA Giovanni: temperature, rainfall, root-zone moisture, topsoil moisture, evaporation, potential evaporation and sunlight
  • Satellite greenness (MODIS EVI) from NASA AppEEARS

For any variable, the player can see the trend over time and test whether it’s significant, with a Mann-Kendall test, Sen’s slope, a 95% confidence interval and a t-test. A false discovery rate correction is applied because many tests run at once. As seen below in Figure 3.

Figure 3: screenshot of the evidence board with all six map pins and the Brandenburg evidence file open in website.

After planting, the game replays the real 2005–2024 record year by year. It shows which stress signals fired, for example a dry summer or a very cold late winter. As seen below in Figure 4.



Figure 4: Screenshot of the Central Spain replay paused in 2015, showing the tree, rainfall chart and stress signals in website.

Each stress rule comes from published Scots pine research and is labelled with its evidence strength. We also tested every rule against the satellite greenness data. Only one held up: dry summer roots (q = 0.007). The game says so openly.

Benefits

  • Makes trend statistics tangible. A p-value becomes “did this tree have a hard year?” Students learn what significance, confidence intervals and multiple testing mean by using them.
  • Honest by design. No data is simulated. Gaps stay gaps. Every claim carries a label: evidence tier, q-value, “no data” or “not a survival forecast”.
  • Free and lightweight. It’s a static website that needs no login, server or installation, and works on any device.
  • Reusable. The pipeline can take any region, and the rules come from a research file in a standard format. A teacher could add a new species or region by changing the configuration.

Intended impact

We want students and the public to understand two things. First, how climate change shows up in a place they care about: Berlin is our home region. Second, how scientists decide whether a change is real or just noise. Many climate tools show trends. Fewer show when the evidence isn’t strong enough. We think learning to say “not shown with this data” is as important as finding a significant result. The tree also connects abstract variables like soil moisture and potential evaporation to something living, which helps with discussions about forest resilience and where to reforest.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • NASA data:
    • GLDAS Noah 0.25° monthly v2.1, through the Giovanni in the Cloud Time Series API
    • MODIS MOD13A3 v061 EVI, through AppEEARS
    • ERA5 temperature from the KNMI Climate Explorer, used as an independent cross-check
    • 17 published Scots pine studies, which supplied the stress thresholds
  • Data pipeline: Python 3 with requests, pandas, NumPy and SciPy, and pymannkendall to validate our statistics
  • Front end: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, D3 for the world map, Plotly for charts, and our own JavaScript statistics engine (checked against SciPy)
  • Hosting: GitHub and GitHub Pages
  • Hardware: standard laptops only
  • AI: We used Claude (Anthropic) as our main assistant for coding, debugging, statistical checks and documentation, and OpenAI Codex (ChatGPT) for some of the coding. All data comes from NASA and partner sources, every AI-assisted step was reviewed and run by the team, and the illustrations are our own hand drawings.

What makes it creative

  • A hand-drawn detective story instead of a dashboard. The player gathers evidence, makes a call and closes the case. This mirrors how a scientist works: hypothesis, evidence, test, verdict.
  • One tree, one seed. Focusing on a single real species gives every variable a purpose. The question becomes “does this stress the tree?”, not “here are seven lines”.
  • Research rules tested against satellites. We didn’t just apply thresholds from the literature. We checked them against MODIS greenness and showed the player which ones failed.
  • A hand-drawn case-file look. Manila folders, rubber stamps and our own detective and magnifying glass illustrations make statistics feel approachable rather than technical.

Factors we considered

  • Data integrity: no invented or gap-filled values. Quality checks run on every series: physical ranges, coverage thresholds, and using the same grid points for every variable.
    • correction for autocorrelation and for multiple tests
    • known biases of the GLDAS data reported openly: potential evaporation runs high, and rainfall is overestimated in snowy regions
    • regions where our temperature trend disagrees with ERA5 flagged in the game
  • Audience: plain-language explanations, plus a species guide and tooltips for students and the public without statistics training.
  • Choice of regions: as different as possible (oceanic, boreal, alpine, Mediterranean, continental steppe and Central European), plus a personal home region.
  • Scope and time: within the 48-hour limit we dropped one data request (Kazakh greenness) rather than fill it with estimates, and labelled the gap.
  • Accessibility and reach: it runs in any browser, is free to host, and needs no account.
